Neonatal individuals of the Highland streaked tenrec (Hemicentetes nigriceps) emerge weighing approximately eight grams [Wwb = approximately eight grams], a remarkably modest body mass given the species' ultimate adult size. This diminutive birth mass reflects the altricial state of the pups, which are born hairless and with closed eyes, entirely dependent on maternal care during the first weeks of life. Reported adult body mass in wild populations spans a considerable range, with fully grown individuals typically attaining between 70 and 160 grams, although the species is generally considered to reach an ultimate wet weight of around 150 grams [Wwi = around 150 grams]. Intraspecific variation in mass is considerable and has been linked to seasonal fluctuations in prey availability, particularly the abundance of oligochaete worms and soft-bodied arthropods that constitute the bulk of the diet at intermediate elevations. The relatively high asymptotic mass of H. nigriceps compared to other species of the genus, such as the smaller Hemicentetes semispinosus, may reflect the energetic demands of a more fossorial lifestyle and the associated costs of maintaining a specialized foraging apparatus, including the elongated snout and powerful forelimbs used to extract subterranean prey from the moist leaf litter of eastern Madagascar's montane rainforests.

Reproductive output in Hemicentetes nigriceps has been quantified under laboratory conditions that mimic the thermal regime of its natural habitat. Females typically produce litters ranging from two to eight pups per reproductive event [N_R_i = two to eight pups per reproductive event], with the modal litter size falling near the middle of this range. The maximum daily reproduction rate, derived from the combination of litter size and the frequency of successive litters, yields an annual reproductive output of approximately five pups per year [Ri = approximately five pups per year] when females are maintained at a stable ambient temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This level of fecundity is modest for an insectivorous mammal of this body size, a pattern that aligns with the relatively slow life-history pace characteristic of tenrecids more broadly. The interbirth interval under these captive conditions is approximately 73 days [F_R_i = approximately 73 days], a figure that likely reflects the considerable energetic investment required to sustain lactation and the rapid post-natal growth of the altricial young through to independence.

Gestation in the Highland streaked tenrec proceeds for a documented period of approximately fifty-nine days [tg = approximately fifty-nine days] when the gravid female is held at a thermoneutral temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], though field estimates place the duration between fifty-five and sixty-three days depending on local thermal conditions and maternal body condition. This gestational period is notably elongated relative to that of other tenrec species of comparable size, potentially reflecting constraints imposed by the species' elevated basal metabolic demands. At a body temperature of 30.9 °C [T = 30.9 °C], the maximum basal metabolic rate for this species was recorded at 72.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 72.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that underscores the relatively low metabolic intensity typical of afrotherian mammals. This comparatively depressed resting metabolism, measured via open-flow respirometry during the inactive phase of the daily cycle, is thought to be an adaptation to the unpredictable resource availability of the montane environment, allowing individuals to conserve energy during periods of food scarcity while maintaining the capacity for rapid digestive throughput when prey is abundant.

Post-natal development proceeds through a series of well-defined ontogenetic stages, each sensitive to the ambient thermal environment. Weaning of the pups, marking the end of nutritional dependence on the mother, occurs at approximately twenty-one days after birth [tx = approximately twenty-one days after birth] when the litter is maintained at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], although field observations indicate a broader range of eighteen to twenty-five days depending on maternal condition and litter size. This relatively early weaning age, compared to other tenrecids of similar mass, may facilitate the rapid turnover of successive litters within a single breeding season. Juveniles then enter a period of rapid somatic growth and behavioral maturation, during which they begin to accompany the mother on foraging excursions and progressively shift from milk to a diet of soil invertebrates. The ability to thermoregulate independently develops gradually over the first weeks of life, and the availability of a warm nest environment is critical for maintaining growth rates that allow the young to reach adult body mass before the onset of the cooler dry season.

Sexual maturity is reached relatively quickly following nutritional independence, with males and females alike attaining puberty at approximately thirty-seven days after birth [tp = approximately thirty-seven days after birth] under a constant thermal regimen of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This rapid maturation, occurring little more than two weeks after weaning, is one of the fastest documented among afrotherian mammals and may be an adaptation to the pronounced seasonality of Madagascar's eastern rainforests, where the window for successful reproduction is tightly constrained by rainfall patterns and prey availability. Despite this early physiological readiness, the maximum lifespan of Hemicentetes nigriceps, extrapolated from captive records of the congeneric Hemicentetes semispinosus maintained under identical thermal conditions of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], is estimated at approximately three years [am = approximately three years]. This relatively short longevity, coupled with early maturation and moderate litter sizes, places the species firmly within a fast life-history strategy compared to other small-bodied afrotherians. Field recapture data from the Ranomafana region suggest that few individuals survive beyond their second breeding season, with predation by the fossorial snake Ithycyphus miniatus and the Malagasy ring-tailed mongoose Galidia elegans representing the primary sources of extrinsic mortality in the wild.
